newsitem.title: FRANCE: French right warms to odd saviours as vote nears.
newsitem.headline: French right warms to odd saviours as vote nears.

text.p: Socially-minded Philippe Seguin and free-marketeer Alain Madelin have emerged as a risky "dream team" for the ruling centre-right three days before the second decisive round of France's parliamentary election.

Opposition Socialist leader Lionel Jospin, sounding increasingly confident of victory on Sunday, was to hold the last big rally of his combative campaign in the northern city of Lille on Thursday night.

In a hint of a blessing, President Jacques Chirac telephoned National Assembly speaker Seguin, a recent convert to a single European currency, and former finance minister Madelin as the two emerged as improbable saviours for the fractious coalition.

Chirac talked with them about the campaign, which came alight after the left stunned the right by winning more votes on the first round on May 25. Seguin and Madelin attended a rally on Wednesday night and said they agreed on essential issues.

But analysts said the bizarre last-minute tandem could alienate as many voters as it attracts by further blurring Chirac's unclear message about what policies he wants a centre-right government to follow in France.

Conservative Chirac called the snap election urging a "new elan" to help France join a single European currency, pledging to stick with austerity to qualify for the euro while stressing social policies to combat record 12.8 percent unemployment.

Seguin has topped opinion polls as the voters' favourite if the centre-right wins. He has been thrust ever more into the limelight after Prime Minister Alain Juppe said he would stand down because of the May 25 mauling.
"We both believe that freedoms are worth nothing if they have no social dimension," Seguin said in a speech with Madelin to about 1,500 people in the Alpine city of Chambery.
With Seguin as prime minister, the outspoken Madelin might regain the job as finance minister he lost in 1995 for attacking civil servants' "privileges".

French financial markets were set for another day of turbulence after plunging on the prospect that the Socialist-led opposition, planning to create 700,000 jobs and cut the working week from 39 hours to 35, would win Sunday's decisive ballot.
Stocks crashed 3.63 percent on Wednesday and the CAC-40 index is 6.5 percent below its level before the left outpolled the right on the May 25 first round.
Former education minister Jospin has sounded increasingly confident, telling his troops to avoid complacency.
Chirac called the election 10 months early, gambling that his coalition allies could win another five years to run in tandem with his own seven-year term ending in 2002.

"Yes, we are ready to govern," Jospin said in Cintegabelle, south-west France. And in a jab at Chirac's gamble gone awry, he said: "One must never be fooled by who is in charge. And in democracy, there is only one sovereign -- the people."

Juppe urged coalition members to go out and try to win those who abstained on the first round vote on Sunday. "It's worth rolling up your sleeves a bit more, it's worth the trouble to go and see everyone...who did not vote," he said.
He also took a swipe at Jospin for saying that he favoured decriminalising hashish in a television interview -- deeply at odds with current policy outlawing all narcotics.
Jospin "was speaking about cannabis. He was asked 'what would you do?' He had this extraordinary reply: 'We mustn't legalise it, but we mustn't punish it either."

Former centrist president Valery Giscard d'Estaing urged a new centre-right government to prepare a new package of social and tax measures in July, aimed at creating economic growth of three percent a year to cut unemployment.
"The central aim from here to Sunday is to say: we want to give work to all French people," he told France 2 television.
